summary: Consonant-final F mostly adopt either -en-, or a zero linker, or -s-. It is possible that there is a tendency to choose by singular/plural meaning: if the second constituent forces the first constituent to take a collective or plural meaning, -en- is more likely (especially in final-stressed F), otherwise mostly a zero linker or -s- is chosen.

evidence.summary: One-syllable F sometimes adopt -en-, sometimes a zero linker. It is possible that there is a tendency to choose by singular/plural meaning.
Consonant-final F adopt -en- less productively.
-(e)n- sometimes has a plural meaning (especially after weak F [1]).

-en- attaches regularly to monosyllabic or polysyllabic final-stressed weak F when the plural interpretation is allowed, with a very few counterexamples. If the plural reading is inadequate, another linking element, mostly -s- or zero, has to be chosen.
F not ending in -e do not usually attach -en-; if there is a singular interpretation, they attach a zero linker.
-(e)n- exhibits a very weak positive effect on plural reading (with non-significant p-value) [2].

footnotes.2: This finding concerning plural interpretability of -(e)n- is not very reliable. -(e)n- may occur after different classes of nouns, and the study indeed included occurrences of -(e)n- after nouns from these different classes. All the occurrences were analyzed altogether disregarding the class of the noun. However, as literature points out, these different classes may have different predispositions towards plural interpretability. Thus for example, the tendency of a plural reading of -(e)n- was pointed out by a few papers for F with a stress on the last syllable (incl. monosyllabic F), which is not the case for trochaic F or weak masculines. Thus, making a single conclusion about all occurrences from different classes adopting -(e)n- may be misleading since strong effect of one class may be wiped out by the absence of the same effect for the others. However, since even with this averaging over the classes, the overall effect is positive (even if weakly), we include this finding in the evidence, assuming the effect of -(e)n- after F with a stress on the last syllable (incl. monosyllabic F) was most probably positive as well.

summary: Nouns ending in schwa regularly adopt -n- if the schwa is not a suffix, this is the only class of words that can attach this linker. If the schwa is a suffix of a deadjective F, -n- and zero linkers are about equally possible. Deverbal F with the schwa suffix mostly attach a zero linker but can attach an -n- when the first constituent has a plural reading.

evidence.summary: F ending in schwa (they are already two-syllabic) regularly adopt -n-.
F ending in schwa adopt -n- if schwa is not a suffix, otherwise a zero linker.
F ending in schwa adopt -n- productively.
The claim that F ending in schwa always attach a zero linker is not supported by the empirical data, but it should be marked as a tendency [1].
-n- occurs only after schwa, and most of the words ending with a schwa adopt it.
F ending in schwa will almost always attach an -n- with a very few exceptions [2].

Nouns (especially weak F) ending in schwa mostly adopt -n-. However, deadjective F ending in a schwa suffix have a zero linker or -n- in about the same number of cases. Deverbative F ending in schwa suffix  mostly have a zero linker; they can attach an -n- though when the first constituent has a plural reading [3, 4].
F ending in schwa virtually always occur with -n-.

footnotes.1: The counterexample there is a deadjective F: tiefe_+n_meter, which is in line with the overall constraint.
footnotes.2: The exception given there is kohle_berg_werk; a variant kohle_+n_berg_werk coexists. Let's consider further counterexample kohle_filter provided here without a coexisting *kohle_+n_filter. Both kohle_berg_werk and kohle_filter can be accounted for if we assume the constraint `tech_term` is stronger than `schwa_f` and thus -- since these are technical terms -- it blocks the application of `schwa_f` in these cases.
footnotes.3: A further claim was made in the paper: 'Finally, further F ending in schwa can adopt an -n- if they denote a concrete countable, even if no plural meaning occurs'. However, these cases simply fall into the cases of F ending in a non-suffix schwa and are only a subset thereof.
footnotes.4: Mixed and irregular M and N ending in schwa also fall here: 'Auge', 'Interesse' can be handled assuming `schwa` > `mixed_mn`. However, many of further examples are eventually overtaken by other constraints: 'Name', 'Glaube'. etc. will be governed by `ens` (assuming `ens` > `schwa`); 'Ende' mostly removes the schwa and is thus not considered in this iteration; 'Gebäude' will be governed by `null_plural` (assuming `null_plural` > `schwa`).

summary: Copulative compounds regularly attach a zero linker.

evidence.summary: The probability of a linking element to appear decreases as the compound type becomes closer to syntax: determinative compounds adopt explicit linkers non-systematically; copulative compounds with additive relations can adopt explicit linkers, but less frequently; copulative compounds with appositive relations systematically adopt a zero linker [1].
Copulative compounds do not attach explicit linkers.
Copulative compounds always have a zero linker. In particular, weak M as well as F ending with suffix -in always adopt -en- unless they are copulative, in which case they have a zero linker [2].

footnotes.1: The author defines two different types of copulative compounds: with additive relations and with appositive relations. However, this notation is not conventional. What the author calls 'copulative compounds with additive relations' are not defined as copulative compounds in most of the literature, while what the author calls 'copulative compounds with appositive relations' are what is defined "usual" copulative compounds. Thus, in our terms this finding can be summarized as 'non-copulative compounds adopt explicit linkers non-systematically, while copulative compounds systematically adopt a zero linker'.

summary: Derivatives forming the plural with a zero ending -- especially with suffixes -er, -ler, -ner, -el, -sel, -chen, -lein -- attach a zero linking element regularly. Derivatives with suffix -en also attach a zero linker with a few exceptions unless they are a deverbative, in which case they always attach -s-. Simplex M and N, as well as any F forming the plural with a zero ending attach a zero linker in majority of cases.

evidence.summary: Derivatives forming the plural with a zero ending -- especially with suffixes -er, -ler, -ner, -el, -sel, -chen, -lein -- attach a zero linking element regularly. Derivatives with suffix -en also attach a zero linker unless they are a deverbative, in which case they mostly attach -s- [1]. Simplex M and N forming the plural with a zero ending attach a zero linker in 90% of cases. F forming the plural with a zero ending attach a zero linker in 85% of cases.

summary: Nouns forming the plural with an -er with or without umlaut (these are mostly N and some M, mostly simplices and never loanwords) mostly attach both a zero linker or =er= in different cases, and this is the only class of words that can attach the latter. =er= is more probable (with counterexamples) when a plural meaning is present, in which case these nouns will indicate concrete, countable entities. footnotes.1: All the examples provided in this source have stressed prefixes.
footnotes.3: The results of `nübling_szczepaniak_2008` (provided again in `nübling_szczepaniak_2013`) are based on a corpus study but are however subject to questions because of the methodology used. First of all, only 21 nouns with unstressed and 19 nouns with stressed prefixes were considered for further combinations, which is a very small sample. Even though the number of resulting compounds was very large, the fact that the same nouns tend to occur with the same linkers (see TODO) discards the representativeness of the large sample size. Furthermore, many of the prefixed nouns were derivates from the same verb (e.g. 'Ansicht', 'Aufsicht', 'Übersicht') which again reduces the diversity of the sample. Furthermore, no specific examples were provided in the paper, whereas further literature suggest several counterexamples to the claim about derivatives with stressed prefixes. Hence, we believe the absolute numbers provided in `nübling_szczepaniak_2008` might not be very reliable. However, these findings may suggest a general trend that prefixed deverbatives with unstressed prefixes tend to attach -s- more often than those with stressed prefixes: verfall_+s_datum vs überfall_kommando.
footnotes.4: Explanation: unstressed prefixes form phonologically bad words. -s- is therefore used to mark the boundary of the phonological word starting with such a suffix.
footnotes.5: Explanation: -s- is used to mark a morphological boundary after a morphologically complex constituent.
